articles.summary: Employee Management How to Plan a Successful End-of-Year Company Retreat Oluwakemi Adesina November 10, 2026 An end-of-year company retreat is a structured offsite event that combines business strategy reflection, team bonding, and employee recognition. A successful retreat requires aligning business objectives, managing logistics tightly, selecting an accessible location, and balancing strategic planning with relaxation to energise teams for the coming year. By November, most Nigerian organizations already planning to wrap up the year. Between navigating volatile market shifts, hitting quarterly revenue targets, and managing end-of-year client sprints, team morale often takes a quiet hit. This is precisely why leadership teams treat an end of year company retreat as an operational reset and not just as an expensive corporate flex. Stepping out of the daily grind allows employees and leadership to decompress, review annual wins, digest hard-earned lessons, and build authentic relationships away from Slack threads and rigid boardrooms. However, there is a fine line between a well-executed retreat that leaves your team energized and a poorly organized getaway that feels like unpaid weekend overtime. A successful retreat requires clear intent, airtight budgeting, and deliberate planning. What Is an End-of-Year Company Retreat? An end-of-year company retreat is a dedicated, offsite gathering designed to bring an organization together away from standard office operations. Unlike a standard evening party or a brief team-building session, a retreat balances structured business reflection with open social connection. End-of-Year Retreat: Multi-faceted offsite combining strategic alignment, performance review, structured team bonding, and relaxation. End-of-Year Party: Social, celebratory event focused almost entirely on leisure, food, and music, usually lasting a few hours. Team-Building Event: Targeted workshop or activity focused strictly on specific group dynamics, communication skills, or problem-solving exercises. Organizing a retreat at the end of the fiscal year provides a natural transition point. Research by HR authorities consistently demonstrates that structured offsites improve cross-departmental trust, reduce Q4 burnout, and reinforce company culture heading into Q1. Set Clear Objectives Before Planning Your Retreat Before booking a single resort room or calling a logistics coordinator, ask a fundamental question: What does success look like when everyone returns to their desks on Monday? Clear retreat objectives typically align around five primary pillars: Reviewing Annual Business Performance: Analyzing key metrics, celebrate milestones, and dissecting operational bottlenecks openly. Recognizing Employee Contributions: Highlighting top performers, celebrating long-term loyalty, and ensuring every team member feels valued. Breaking Down Functional Silos: Creating opportunities for engineering, sales, operations, and finance team to interact naturally without work pressure. Setting Q1 and Annual Priorities: Aligning the entire company around core business objectives for the coming year. Decompressing & Reconnecting: Giving employees breathing room to recharge mentally after a grueling operational year. How to Create a Realistic Company Retreat Budget Creating a company retreat budget requires factoring in every expense line item early to avoid mid-planning surprises. When budgeting for a Nigerian retreat, finance leads must account for: · Venue hire & conference hall facility charges · Accommodation (single vs. shared room allocations) · Intercity transportation, fuel, or charter bus logistics · Full-board meal packages, snacks, and evening social refreshments · Facilitator fees & specialized team building activities in Nigeria · Employee recognition awards, custom swag, and gift packages · Emergency contingency funds (always budget 10%–15% buffer for inflation or unexpected expenses) A Sample Retreat Budget Framework This is an illustrative financial framework for planning offsites across different team sizes: Company Size Format & Duration Key Expense Focus Sample Total Budget Range (NGN)* Small Team (10–25) 1-Day Local Offsite Day resort, meals, transport, facilitator ₦2.5M – ₦5.0M Medium Team (26–70) 2-Day Overnight Mid-tier resort, accommodation, full board, activities ₦8.0M – ₦18.0M Large Enterprise (70+) 3-Day Full Retreat Destination resort, charter logistics, gala, customized swag ₦25.0M – ₦50.0M+ Note: All figures are illustrative financial benchmarks provided for operational planning and do not represent fixed market vendor quotes. Choose the Right Retreat Location in Nigeria Location sets the tone for your entire retreat. Choosing a destination requires balancing travel convenience with a genuine change of environment: · Travel Friction: Avoid spending 6 hours in traffic for a 1-day retreat. · Facility Infrastructure: Ensure reliable power backup, high-speed internet for presentations, and clean conference setups. · Recreational Variety: Check for outdoor spaces, swimming facilities, or beach access to support leisure hours. Prominent corporate getaway Nigeria destinations to evaluate include: · Lagos & Surrounding Outskirts: Ideal for short getaways (e.g., Lekki peninsula resorts, Epe beach estates, or Badagry heritage sites). · Oyo State (Ibadan): Offers serene, budget-friendly environments with historic conference centers and eco-resorts. · Ogun State (Abeokuta): Provides scenic hill resorts and quiet golf retreats within easy driving distance from Lagos. · Abuja & FCT Outskirts: Excellent infrastructure, high-end hospitality hubs, and tranquil rock-side resorts for northern teams. · Cross River (Calabar) & Akwa Ibom (Uyo): Pristine nature resorts, rich cultural hospitality, and top-tier conference infrastructure for multi-day national retreats. Plan Activities That Encourage Team Engagement A great retreat strikes a delicate balance between work and play. Structuring your schedule around four core activity tracks keeps energy high: Team-Building Activities Move past generic trust falls. Design collaborative end of year team building activities like problem-solving scavenger hunts, cross-functional hackathons, or strategic escape room challenges that mirror workplace problem-solving. Employee Recognition Activities Use the retreat setting to publicly celebrate excellence. Present awards for innovation, resilience, leadership, and long service. Public recognition reinforces organizational culture and signals that hard work is noticed. Business Reflection Sessions Dedicate clear, time-boxed blocks to review annual performance candidly. Encourage transparent feedback on what worked, what failed, and how processes can improve in Q1. Relaxation and Social Activities Leave un-programed room for downtime. Bonfires, casual games, guided nature walks, or live music evenings allow colleagues to form genuine personal connections without work deadlines hovering over them. Create a Practical End-of-Year Retreat Agenda Pacing is everything. Overloading the itinerary leads to fatigue, while under-scheduling leads to aimless wandering. ("Neurotech"), strengthening our portfolio of products in retinal disease Ad Hoc Announcement Pursuant to Art. 53 LR GENEVA--(BUSINESS WIRE)-- Alcon (SIX/NYSE:ALC), the global leader in eye care, reported its financial results for the three and nine month periods ending September 30, 2026. For the third quarter of 2026, sales were $2.7 billion, up 5% on a reported and constant currency basis1, as compared to the same quarter of the previous year. Alcon reported diluted earnings per share of $0.54 and core diluted earnings per share2 of $0.91 in the third quarter of 2026. "We remain on track for our 2026 objectives with year-to-date sales growth of six percent and double-digit core EPS growth, despite some specific areas of competitive pressure,” said David J. Endicott, Alcon’s Chief Executive Officer. “We are encouraged by the momentum across our newest products and the strength of our pipeline. The breadth of our portfolio of innovation together with the recent acquisition of Neurotech, positions us well to drive sustainable long-term growth." Third-quarter and first nine months of 2026 results Reported net sales for the third quarter of 2026 were $2.7 billion, up 5% on both a reported and constant currency basis versus the third quarter of 2025. Reported net sales for the first nine months of 2026 were $8.2 billion, up 7% versus the first nine months of 2025. Excluding favorable currency impacts of 1%, sales were up 6% on a constant currency basis. Implantables net sales were $422 million, a decrease of 2% on both a reported and constant currency basis. This reflects a decrease in IOLs of 1% constant currency, due to competitive pressures in the U.S. This decline was partially offset by strong PanOptix Pro performance and growth in international markets. Consumables net sales were $789 million, an increase of 6% on both a reported and constant currency basis. Growth was driven by procedural volumes, price increases and Valeda consumables. Equipment/other net sales were $269 million, an increase of 11% on both a reported and constant currency basis. This growth was led by equipment launches, including the Unity platform and Valeda . Vision Care Vision Care net sales were $1.2 billion, an increase of 6% on both a reported and constant currency basis versus the third quarter of 2025. Contact lenses net sales were $737 million, an increase of 4%. Excluding unfavorable currency impacts of 1%, Contact lenses net sales increased 5% constant currency. This growth reflects favorable mix of premium products as well as price increases, particularly in the U.S., and was partially offset by declines in legacy products. Ocular health net sales were $500 million, an increase of 8% on both a reported and constant currency basis. This growth was led by our portfolio of dry eye products, including Tryptyr and Systane, partially offset by declines in contact lens care. Nine months Surgical Surgical net sales were $4.5 billion, an increase of 7% on a reported basis and 6% on a constant currency basis versus the first nine months of 2025. Implantables net sales were $1.3 billion, an increase of 1%. Excluding favorable currency impacts of 1%, Implantables net sales were in line with the prior year period in constant currency. IOLs increased 1% constant currency, primarily driven by growth in international markets and strong PanOptix Pro performance, partially offset by competitive pressures in the U.S. In addition, there were lower sales in surgical glaucoma. Consumables net sales were $2.4 billion, an increase of 7%. Excluding favorable currency impacts of 2%, Consumables net sales increased 5% constant currency. Growth was driven by procedural volumes, price increases and Valeda consumables. Equipment/other net sales were $801 million, an increase of 21%. Excluding favorable currency impacts of 2%, Equipment/other net sales increased 19% constant currency. This growth was led by equipment launches, including the Unity platform and Valeda . Vision Care Vision Care net sales were $3.7 billion, an increase of 8% on a reported basis and 7% on a constant currency basis versus the first nine months of 2025. Contact lenses net sales were $2.2 billion, an increase of 5% on both a reported and constant currency basis. This growth reflects favorable mix of premium products as well as price increases, particularly in the U.S., and was partially offset by declines in legacy products. Ocular health net sales were $1.5 billion, an increase of 11%. Excluding favorable currency impacts of 1%, Ocular health net sales increased 10% constant currency. Growth was led by our portfolio of dry eye products, including Tryptyr and Systane . Operating income Third quarter Operating income was $381 million (+15%, +15% cc), compared to $332 million in the prior year period. Operating margin was 14.0% compared to 12.8% in the prior year period and increased 1.2 percentage points on both a reported and constant currency basis. The current year period included tariff refunds of $58 million, lower amortization and manufacturing efficiencies, partially offset by a charge for fair value adjustments to contingent consideration liabilities, costs associated with efficiency measures and increased sales and marketing spend. Adjustments to arrive at core operating income in the current year period were $210 million, mainly due to $131 million of amortization, $38 million for fair value adjustments to contingent consideration liabilities and $36 million of costs associated with efficiency measures. Adjustments to arrive at core operating income in the prior year period were $191 million, mainly due to $176 million of amortization and $13 million of acquisition and integration related items. Core operating income was $591 million (+13%, +13% cc), compared to $523 million in the prior year period. Core operating margin was 21.8% compared to 20.2% in the prior year period and increased 1.6 percentage points on a reported basis and 1.5 percentage points on a constant currency basis. The current year period included tariff refunds and manufacturing efficiencies, partially offset by increased sales and marketing spend. Nine months Operating income was $684 million (-35%, -37% cc), compared to $1.0 billion in the prior year period. Operating margin was 8.4% compared to 13.7% in the prior year period and decreased 5.3 percentage points on a reported basis and 5.6 percentage points on a constant currency basis. The current year period included a pre-tax, non-cash net charge of $402 million related to the decision to discontinue the IOL programs acquired from PowerVision, Inc. in March 2019 ("PowerVision programs"), costs associated with efficiency measures, increased sales and marketing spend, impairment charges related to a currently marketed product intangible asset, a charge for fair value adjustments to contingent consideration liabilities and the impact from ongoing tariffs, partially offset by lower amortization, tariff refunds, manufacturing efficiencies and price increases. The prior year period included gains on fair value remeasurements of investments in associated companies, partially offset by charges related to the discontinued commercialization of a Vision Care product. Adjustments to arrive at core operating income in the current year period were $1.1 billion, mainly due to a pre-tax, non-cash net charge of $402 million related to the discontinuation of the PowerVision programs, $388 million of amortization, $157 million of costs associated with efficiency measures, $38 million of impairment charges related to a currently marketed product intangible asset, $38 million for fair value adjustments to contingent consideration liabilities and $24 million of acquisition and integration related items. Adjustments to arrive at core operating income in the prior year period were $478 million, mainly due to $521 million of amortization, $44 million of product discontinuation charges and $36 million of acquisition and integration related items, partially offset by gains of $142 million on fair value remeasurements of investments in associated companies. Core operating income was $1.7 billion (+14%, +12% cc), compared to $1.5 billion in the prior year period. Core operating margin was 21.2% compared to 20.0% in the prior period and increased 1.2 percentage points on a reported basis and 1.1 percentage points on a constant currency basis. The current year period included tariff refunds, manufacturing efficiencies and price increases, partially offset by increased sales and marketing spend and the impact from ongoing tariffs. Taxes Third quarter Reported tax expense was $68 million, compared to $46 million in the prior year period, and the average reported tax rate was 20.7%, compared to 16.3% in the prior year period. Core tax expense was $96 million, compared to $80 million in the prior year period, and the average core tax rate was 17.8%, compared to 16.9% in the prior year period. The average reported tax rate in the current year period was impacted by the non-deductible fair value adjustments to contingent consideration liabilities. In addition, both the average reported and core tax rates in the current year period were higher primarily driven by higher discrete tax benefits in the prior year period and more favorable mix of pre-tax income/(loss) across geographical tax jurisdictions in the current year period. Nine months Reported tax expense was $73 million, compared to $133 million in the prior year period, and the average reported tax rate was 14.0%, compared to 14.8% in the prior year period. The average reported tax rate in the current year period was impacted by a $115 million tax benefit from the reversal of deferred tax liabilities related to the discontinuation of the PowerVision programs and the non-taxable fair value adjustments to contingent consideration liabilities. The average reported tax rate in the prior year period included a non-taxable gain on the fair value remeasurement of an investment in an associated company and net benefits from discrete tax items. Core tax expense was $305 million, compared to $240 million in the prior year period, and the average core tax rate was 19.4%, compared to 17.4% in the prior year period. The prior year period included net benefits from discrete tax items. Diluted earnings per share Third quarter Diluted earnings per share of $0.54 increased 13%, or 14% on a constant currency basis. Core diluted earnings per share of $0.91 increased 15% on both a reported and constant currency basis, versus the prior year period. Nine months Diluted earnings per share of $0.92 decreased 40%, or 43% on a constant currency basis, versus the prior year period, primarily due to a post-tax, non-cash net charge of approximately $287 million related to the discontinuation of the PowerVision programs and costs associated with efficiency measures. The prior year period included gains of $142 million on fair value remeasurements of investments in associated companies. Core diluted earnings per share of $2.60 increased 14%, or 11% on a constant currency basis, versus the prior year period. Capital allocation The Company returned $210 million to shareholders in the third quarter through share repurchases. As of September 30, 2026, the Company had approximately $1.0 billion remaining of its previously announced $1.5 billion authorization. On a year-to-date basis through the third quarter, the Company has returned $748 million to shareholders through dividends and share repurchases. our success in completing strategic acquisitions, including equity investments in early-stage companies, on favorable terms or at all, and in integrating acquired businesses; the success of our research and development efforts, including our ability to innovate to compete effectively; our ability to manage the rapid evolution and adoption of artificial intelligence; terrorism, war and similar events; our ability to forecast sales demand and manage our inventory levels and the changing buying patterns of our customers; pricing pressure from changes in third party payor coverage and reimbursement methodologies; our ability to comply with all laws to which we may be subject; the ability to obtain regulatory clearance and approval of our products as well as compliance with any post-approval obligations, including quality control of our manufacturing; the effect of product recalls or voluntary market withdrawals; our ability to manage social impact and sustainability matters; our ability to properly educate and train healthcare providers on our products; our ability to protect our intellectual property; the accuracy of our accounting estimates and assumptions, including pension and other post-employment benefit plan obligations and the carrying value of intangible assets, and the adequacy of our financial reporting, accounting practices and internal controls; our ability to service our debt obligations; the need for additional financing through the issuance of debt or equity; the effects of litigation, including product liability lawsuits and governmental investigations; legislative, tax and regulatory reform; the impact of being listed on two stock exchanges; the ability to declare and pay dividends; the different rights afforded to our shareholders as a Swiss corporation compared to a US corporation; the effect of maintaining or losing our foreign private issuer status under US securities laws; and the ability to enforce US judgments against Swiss corporations. Non-IFRS measures as defined by the Company Alcon uses certain non-IFRS metrics when measuring performance, including when measuring current period results against prior periods, including core results, percentage changes measured in constant currency, EBITDA, free cash flow and net (debt)/liquidity. Because of their non-standardized definitions, the non-IFRS measures (unlike IFRS measures) may not be comparable to the calculation of similar measures of other companies. These supplemental non-IFRS measures are presented solely to permit investors to more fully understand how Alcon management assesses underlying performance. These supplemental non-IFRS measures are not, and should not be viewed as, a substitute for IFRS measures. Core results Alcon core results, including core operating income and core net income, exclude all amortization and impairment charges of intangible assets, excluding software, all fair value adjustments to contingent considerations from acquisitions, other than changes due to the time value of money, product discontinuation charges, net gains and losses on fund investments and equity securities valued at fair value through profit and loss ("FVPL"), fair value adjustments of financial assets in the form of options to acquire a company carried at FVPL, fair value remeasurements of investments in associated companies and certain acquisition related items. The following items that exceed a threshold of $10 million, are not operating expenses necessary to the operation of the business and have costs that will vary over periods and are also excluded from core results: integration and divestment related income and expenses, divestment gains and losses, restructuring charges/releases and related items, legal related items, gains/losses on early extinguishment of debt or debt modifications, past service costs for post-employment benefit plans, impairments of property, plant and equipment and software, as well as income and expense items that management deems exceptional and that are or are expected to accumulate within the year to be over a $10 million threshold. Taxes on the adjustments between IFRS and core results take into account, for each individual item included in the adjustment, the tax rate that will finally be applicable to the item based on the jurisdiction where the adjustment will finally have a tax impact. Generally, this results in amortization and impairment of intangible assets and acquisition-related restructuring and integration items having a full tax impact. There is usually a tax impact on other items, although this is not always the case for certain items such as legal settlements in certain jurisdictions. Alcon believes that investor understanding of its performance is enhanced by disclosing core measures of performance because, since they exclude items that can vary significantly from period to period, the core measures enable a helpful comparison of business performance across periods. For this same reason, Alcon uses these core measures in addition to IFRS and other measures as important factors in assessing its performance. A limitation of the core measures is that they provide a view of Alcon operations without including all events during a period, such as the effects of an acquisition, divestment, or amortization/impairments of purchased intangible assets and restructurings. Constant currency Changes in the relative values of non-US currencies to the US dollar can affect Alcon's financial results and financial position. To provide additional information that may be useful to investors, including changes in sales volume, we present information about changes in our net sales and various values relating to operating and net income that are adjusted for such foreign currency effects. Constant currency calculations have the goal of eliminating two exchange rate effects so that an estimate can be made of underlying changes in the Consolidated Income Statement excluding: the impact of translating the income statements of consolidated entities from their non-US dollar functional currencies to the US dollar; and the impact of exchange rate movements on the major transactions of consolidated entities performed in currencies other than their functional currency. Alcon calculates constant currency measures by translating the current year's foreign currency values for sales and other income statement items into US dollars, using the average exchange rates from the historical comparative period and comparing them to the values from the historical comparative period in US dollars. EBITDA Alcon defines earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortization ("EBITDA") as net income excluding income taxes, depreciation of property, plant and equipment (including any related impairment charges), depreciation of right-of-use assets, amortization of intangible assets (including any related impairment charges), interest expense and other financial income and expense. Alcon management primarily uses EBITDA together with net (debt)/liquidity to monitor leverage associated with financial debts. Free cash flow Alcon defines free cash flow as net cash flows from operating activities less cash flow associated with the purchase or sale of property, plant and equipment. Free cash flow is presented as additional information because Alcon management believes it is a useful supplemental indicator of Alcon's ability to operate without reliance on additional borrowing or use of existing cash. Free cash flow is not intended to be a substitute measure for net cash flows from operating activities as determined under IFRS. Net (debt)/liquidity Alcon defines net (debt)/liquidity as current and non-current financial debt less cash and cash equivalents, current investments, including time deposits, and derivative financial instruments. Net (debt)/liquidity is presented as additional information because management believes it is a useful supplemental indicator of Alcon's ability to pay dividends, to meet financial commitments and to invest in new strategic opportunities, including strengthening its balance sheet. Growth rate and margin calculations For ease of understanding, Alcon uses a sign convention for its growth rates such that a reduction in operating expenses or losses compared to the prior year is shown as a positive growth. Gross margins, core gross margins, operating income margins and core operating income margins are calculated based upon net sales unless otherwise noted. These items are uncertain, depend on many factors and could have a material impact on our IFRS results for the guidance period.
